Introduction to Networks

Chapter 1: Exploring the Network

How networks connect our world: networks of many sizes, network components, media and topologies, LANs, WANs and the Internet, converged and reliable networks with QoS and security, and the changing network environment.

★ Revision kit — Chapter 1: Exploring the Network

Eight structured sections for revision: overview, definitions, concept explanations, comparisons, important facts, a knowledge check, common misunderstandings and a quick revision read. Everything here is additive — the complete original slides follow below, unchanged, and every fact links back to its source slide.

From the course PDFsgrounded in the source slides (linked) Study notesupplementary wording written for this site Practicerevision questions — not lecturer or exam questions

1Chapter overviewFrom the course PDFs

Chapter 1 sets the scene for the whole course: what networks are, why they matter in daily life, and what a network is actually made of. It moves from networks of many sizes (personal to Internet-scale) through the building blocks — end devices, intermediary devices, media and services — to the two main network types (LAN and WAN) and the Internet. It then treats the network as a platform that must be fault tolerant, scalable, secure and able to provide Quality of Service, and closes with home networking trends plus the chapter's security threats and solutions.

Learning objectives

  • Explain how networks support the way we learn, communicate, work and play (slide 4).
  • Identify the three categories of network components — devices, media and services — and give examples of end devices and intermediary devices (slides 9–12).
  • Distinguish LANs, WANs and the Internet, and describe how remote users and businesses connect to the Internet (slides 15–22).
  • Describe the four characteristics of modern network architectures: fault tolerance, scalability, QoS and security (slide 25).
  • List common external security threats and the security components used against them (slides 39–40).

Most important concepts

  • Network components — devices, media and services (three categories).
  • LAN vs WAN — the two most common network infrastructures.
  • Converged networks — one network carrying voice, video and data.
  • Fault tolerance & packet switching — redundancy and alternative routes keep traffic flowing.
  • QoS — matching packet priority to the type of communication.
  • Network vs information security — protecting devices, and protecting the data they carry.

2Key definitionsFrom the course PDFs

LANLocal Area Network

Interconnects end devices in a limited area (home, school, office building or campus), is usually administered by a single organization, and provides high-speed bandwidth to its devices. slide 17

WANWide Area Network

Interconnects LANs over wide geographical areas (between cities, countries or continents), is usually administered by multiple service providers, and typically provides slower-speed links between LANs. slide 18

Internet

A conglomerate — a 'network of networks' — not owned by any individual or group; communication across it relies on common standards from organizations such as the IETF, ICANN and IAB. slide 19

IETFInternet Engineering Task Force

One of the standards organizations that develop the open technologies and standards enabling communication across the Internet. slide 19

ICANNInternet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers

Standards/governance organization named in the chapter as part of keeping the Internet's naming and addressing consistent. slide 19

End device (host)

A source or destination of messages on the network — computers, printers, VoIP phones, cameras, mobile devices. Each host is identified by an address so other hosts can specify it as a destination. slide 10

Intermediary device

Connects end devices to the network or links networks: network access devices (switches, wireless access points), internetworking devices (routers) and security devices (firewalls). slide 11

QoSQuality of Service

Mechanisms that give time-sensitive or business-critical communication higher priority (and undesired traffic lower priority or none), so packet handling matches the type of communication. slide 29

Fault tolerance

The ability to keep traffic flowing when components fail, achieved with redundant links and alternative routes. slide 25

Scalability

A network design that can add more users and devices without performance degrading. slide 25

Converged network

A single network infrastructure carrying voice, video and data together instead of separate purpose-built networks. slide 24

DoSDenial of Service attack

Listed among the most common external threats to networks; an attack that disrupts service rather than stealing data. slide 39

ACLAccess Control List

Listed as a network-security component used to filter traffic as part of security solutions. slide 40

VPNVirtual Private Network

Listed among security components as providing secure access to remote users. slide 40

IPSIntrusion Prevention System

A security component named in the chapter's security-solutions slide. slide 40

3Concept explanationsStudy note

Client, server — or both? slide 6

A device's role is decided by its software, not by the hardware. The same computer can request web pages (client behaviour) and store/deliver e-mail (server behaviour). In peer-to-peer models, devices act as both at the same time.

Example: A laptop with a web browser is a client when it requests a page; the machine holding the website is the server for that request.

Why packet switching beat circuit switching for reliability slide 27

In a circuit-switched network a dedicated path is reserved; if a link on that path fails, the call drops. Packet-switched networks cut messages into packets that can take any available route, so redundancy gives alternative paths — this is what makes networks fault tolerant.

Example: A failed link only costs the packets in flight; the rest reroute instead of the whole session dying.

QoS is prioritising, not adding capacity slide 29

QoS does not create bandwidth — it decides which traffic gets served first. Telephony and video are time-sensitive and get priority; e-mail and web retrieval can wait; peer-to-peer file sharing may be dropped entirely.

Example: During a video conference, the router treats voice packets ahead of a background software update.

Two security concerns, three primary requirements slide 33

The chapter splits security into network infrastructure security (physically secure devices and their management software) and information security (protecting data in packets and at rest). To achieve security it lists three requirements: confidentiality (only authorized recipients read the data — passwords and encryption), integrity (data not altered in transit), and availability (timely, reliable access for authorized users).

Example: Firewalls and antivirus support availability/integrity; encryption and passwords support confidentiality.

Networks of many sizes slide 5

The chapter scales the picture from a simple two-computer network up to the Internet — the largest network, described as a 'network of networks'. The same components and standards work at every size.

Example: A home Wi-Fi LAN and the global Internet use the same end-device / intermediary device / media structure.

Technical terms are kept exactly as the course uses them; the plain-language wording and examples are supplementary study notes.

5Important factsFrom the course PDFs

  • There are three categories of network components: devices, media, services. slide 9
  • Every host on a network is identified by an address; a host that initiates communication uses the destination host's address. slide 10
  • Intermediary devices: switches and wireless access points (network access), routers (internetworking), firewalls (security). slide 11
  • Network media carry signals as electrical impulses, light impulses or electromagnetic waves. slide 12
  • A topology diagram shows the physical location of intermediary devices, configured ports and cable installation, and identifies devices, ports and the IP addressing scheme. slide 14
  • Four architecture characteristics: fault tolerance, scalability, QoS, security. slide 25
  • Security has two concerns: network infrastructure security and information security; three primary requirements: confidentiality, integrity, availability. slide 33
  • Common external threats: viruses, worms, Trojan horses; spyware/adware; zero-day attacks; hacker attacks; DoS attacks; data interception and theft; identity theft. slide 39
  • Security solutions: antivirus/antispyware, firewall filtering, dedicated firewall systems, ACLs, IPS, VPNs. slide 40
  • Home connection technologies named: powerline networking, wireless broadband (WISP dish/antenna; cellular-style fixed wireless), alongside DSL and cable. slide 36
  • The routing and switching platform is described as the foundation of any network infrastructure. slide 42

6Knowledge checkPractice

8 practice questions — a mix of multiple-choice, true/false, short-answer and explanation tasks. Answers stay hidden until you reveal them, and each one explains why it is correct. These are revision questions written for this site from the course content — they are not lecturer instructions or examination questions.

Multiple choiceQ1. According to the chapter, how many categories of network components are there, and what are they?

  • A. Two: hardware and software
  • B. Three: devices, media and services
  • C. Four: end devices, routers, switches and firewalls
  • D. Three: LANs, WANs and the Internet
Show answer & explanation

Answer: B — Three: devices, media and services

Why: The Components of a Network slide names exactly three categories: devices, media and services (slide 9).

True or falseQ2. A WAN is usually administered by a single organization and offers high-speed links to internal devices.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: False

Why: That describes a LAN. WANs interconnect LANs over wide areas, are usually administered by multiple service providers, and typically provide slower-speed links (slides 17–18).

True or falseQ3. In a packet-switched network, redundancy allows alternative routes, which is a basis for fault tolerance.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: True

Why: Fault tolerance in packet-switched networks comes from redundant paths; if one route fails, packets can travel another (slides 25–27).

Short answerQ4. Name the four basic characteristics modern network architectures must address.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Fault tolerance, scalability, Quality of Service (QoS), and security.

Why: Slide 25 lists these four to meet user expectations as networks evolve.

Short answerQ5. What determines whether a device acts as a client, a server, or both?

Show answer & explanation

Answer: The software on the device.

Why: Slide 6: 'The software on a device determines its role' — e.g. browser software makes a device a client for web pages, e-mail server software makes it a server for mail.

Multiple choiceQ6. Which list matches the chapter's three primary requirements for network security?

  • A. Confidentiality, integrity, availability
  • B. Authentication, authorization, accounting
  • C. Antivirus, firewall, VPN
  • D. Fault tolerance, scalability, QoS
Show answer & explanation

Answer: A — Confidentiality, integrity, availability

Why: Slide 33 lists ensuring confidentiality, maintaining communication integrity and ensuring availability as the three primary requirements (B is an AAA triple from a later module, C are solution examples, D are architecture characteristics).

ExplanationQ7. Explain why giving telephony and video higher priority than web page retrieval is a QoS decision, and what QoS is not.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Time-sensitive communication needs packets delivered promptly, so QoS raises its priority and lowers that of non-time-sensitive traffic such as web or e-mail. QoS is prioritising existing capacity — it does not increase bandwidth.

Why: Slide 29 gives exactly these priority examples: increase priority for telephony/video, decrease for web retrieval/e-mail. QoS = matching packet priority to communication type (slide 25).

ExplanationQ8. Using the chapter's examples, describe the difference between network infrastructure security and information security.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Network infrastructure security means physically securing devices and preventing unauthorized access to the management software on them; information security means protecting the data inside packets in transit and data stored on network-attached devices.

Why: Slide 32 defines these two types of security concerns; the following slide adds the confidentiality/integrity/availability requirements that implement them.

7Common misunderstandingsStudy note

Confusing client/server with a type of device

Client and server are roles defined by software, not hardware classes. The same device can be both — the chapter's peer-to-peer slide exists for exactly this reason (slide 6–7).

"The Internet" vs "a network"

The Internet is not one network owned by someone; it is a conglomerate of networks ('network of networks') kept interoperable by shared standards (slides 19, 41). A LAN, by contrast, is usually run by one organization.

QoS = more bandwidth?

No. QoS is about priority decisions — which packets get served first or are blocked. More bandwidth is a capacity change; QoS is a scheduling policy (slides 25, 29).

Security = just antivirus

The chapter separates infrastructure and information security and requires confidentiality, integrity and availability. Antivirus is only one listed component next to firewalls, ACLs, IPS and VPNs (slides 32–40).

8Quick revision (2–5 minutes)Study note

  • Scale: networks from two computers to the Internet ('network of networks'); the Internet's standards come from bodies like IETF, ICANN, IAB.
  • Components: devices (end devices + intermediary: switches/WAPs, routers, firewalls), media (electrical/light/wireless signals), services.
  • Roles: client/server/both — set by software; hosts are identified by addresses.
  • Types: LAN = limited area, one administrator, fast; WAN = wide area, multiple providers, slower links. Also MAN, WLAN, SAN. The Internet interconnects them all.
  • Platform requirements (4): fault tolerance (redundant, packet-switched routes), scalability (grow without degrading), QoS (prioritise time-sensitive traffic), security (infrastructure + information; confidentiality, integrity, availability).
  • Changing environment: home trends (powerline, wireless broadband) and threats (viruses/worms/Trojans, spyware, zero-day, hackers, DoS, interception, identity theft) countered by antivirus, firewalls, ACLs, IPS, VPNs.

Components of a Network

End Devices

Some examples of end devices are:

  • Computers (work stations, laptops, file servers, web servers), network printers, VoIP phones, Security cameras, Mobile handheld devices
  • A host device is either the source or destination of a message transmitted over the network, as shown in the animation. In order to distinguish one host from another, each host on a network is identified by an address. When a host initiates communication, it uses the address of the destination host to specify where the message should be sent.

Supporting Network Architecture

As networks evolve, we are discovering that there are four basic

characteristics that the underlying architectures need to address in order to

meet user expectations:

  • Fault Tolerance (redundancy allows alternative routes)
  • Scalability (add extra users without performance degrading)
  • Quality of Service (QoS) (package priorities match type of communication)
  • Security (software and hardware security)

Providing QoS

Examples of priority decisions for an organization might include:

  • Time-sensitive communication - increase priority for services like telephony or video distribution.
  • Non time-sensitive communication - decrease priority for web page retrieval or email.
  • High importance to organization - increase priority for production control or business transaction data.
  • Undesirable communication - decrease priority or block unwanted activity, like peer-to-peer file sharing or live entertainment.

Providing Network Security

There are two types of network security concerns that must be

addressed:

  • network infrastructure security - physical securing of devices and preventing unauthorized access to the management software that resides on them.
  • information security - protecting the information contained within the packets being transmitted over the network and the information stored on network attached devices

Slide 33
Reliable Network

Providing Network Security

In order to achieve network security, there are three primary

requirements:

  • Ensuring confidentiality - only the intended and authorized recipients - individuals, processes, or devices can access and read data. This is accomplished by having passwords and encrypting data..
  • Maintaining communication integrity - having the assurance that the information has not been altered in transmission, from origin to destination.
  • Ensuring availability - having the assurance of timely and reliable access to data services for authorized users. Network firewall devices, along with desktop and server antivirus software can ensure system reliability.

Networking Technologies for the Home

Wireless Broadband

Wireless Internet Service Provider (WISP)

  • Commonly found in rural environments where DSL or cable services are not available.
  • A small dish or antenna is installed on the subscriber’s roof in range of the WISP transmitter. The connection between the antenna and the WISP is wireless.

Wireless Broadband Service

  • It uses the same technology that cellular technologies like smart phone and tablets are using. An antenna is installed outside the house providing either wireless or wired connectivity for devices in the home. In many areas, home wireless broadband is competing directly with DSL and cable services.

Network Security

Security Threats

The most common external threats to networks include:

  • Viruses, worms, and Trojan horses
  • Spyware and adware
  • Zero-day attacks, also called zero-hour attacks
  • Hacker attacks
  • Denial of service (DoS) attacks
  • Data interception and theft
  • Identity theft

Chapter 1 Summary

2 slides
Slide 41
Exploring the Networking

Summary

In this chapter, you learned:

  • Networks and the Internet have changed the way we communicate, learn, work, and even play.
  • Networks come in all sizes. They can range from simple networks consisting of two computers, to networks connecting millions of devices.
  • The Internet is the largest network in existence. In fact, the term Internet means a ‘network of networks. The Internet provides the services that enable us to connect and communicate with our families, friends, work, and interests.
  • The network infrastructure is the platform that supports the network. It provides the stable and reliable channel over which communication can occur. It is made up of network components including end devices, intermediate devices, and network media.

Slide 42
Exploring the Networking

Summary (cont.)

In this chapter, you learned:

  • Networks must be reliable.
  • Network security is an integral part of computer networking, regardless of whether the network is limited to a home environment with a single connection to the Internet, or as large as a corporation with thousands of users.
  • The network infrastructure can vary greatly in terms of size, number of users, and number and types of services that are supported on it. The network infrastructure must grow and adjust to support the way the network is used. The routing and switching platform is the foundation of any network infrastructure.
